From Batten 1984: There appear to be three layers composing the wall in this species. An outer layer, supposedly of calcite, is composed of very fine, fibrous prisms that are either normal to the outer surface (Figure 2A) or at an angle to it. The prisms are arranged normal to the inner whorl surface. The general appearance is that of asbestoslike coarse myostracum. In contrast to ends of aragonite prism crystals, each crystal terminates in a rhombic cap (Figure 2B). Each of these elongate crystals are undulate with peculiar rounded bosses apparently scattered randomly on the surfaces. 

The middle layer is composed of a single unit of crossed-lamellar structure (Figure 2C). The inner layer is the thinnest and is also composed of prisms resembling myostracum. Both of these prismatic layers are said to be calcitic and the manner of preservation in the material studied supports this conclusion. Of the 21 specimens examined, all show the outer and inner layer intact, with the middle layer leached out completely in most of the specimens, although a few had enough of the middle layer preserved to identify it.  PJW: The "classic" euomphalomorph would have been fairly immobile, particularly in the adult form. However, many show very trochiform shells that likely reflect mobile forms, often with very tangential apertures indicating "fast" crawling (for snails). Some Straparollus species shift from trochiform in early whorls (but post-protoconch) to broach, planispiral shells, which strongly suggests an ecological shift over ontogeny.
